error: JSON object requested, multiple (or no) rows returned
meaning: You called .single() and the query returned zero rows or more than one (PostgREST code PGRST116). .single() insists on exactly one row.
causes: The row does not exist yet, e.g. a profile row that was never created after signup.
RLS hides the row from this user, so the query sees zero rows.
The filter matches several rows because the column is not unique.
An insert/update with .select().single() affected zero rows because a policy blocked it.

steps.text: If 'no row' is a normal case, use .maybeSingle(), which returns data: null instead of an error.
If you expect exactly one row, make the column unique so duplicates cannot happen.
steps.code: alter table public.profiles add constraint profiles_user_unique unique (user_id);

steps.text: Create profile rows automatically on signup with a trigger.
Check RLS: make sure a SELECT policy lets the user see their own row, for example using (auth.uid() = id).
For existing users with no profile, backfill once.
steps.code: insert into public.profiles (id) select id from auth.users on conflict do nothing;

prompt: Supabase throws PGRST116 'JSON object requested, multiple (or no) rows returned'. Find every .single() call; switch to .maybeSingle() wherever the row may not exist and handle null. Add a Postgres trigger that creates a profiles row for each new auth user, backfill missing profiles, and add a unique constraint on the column we filter by. Make sure there is a SELECT RLS policy using auth.uid().

faq.a: Use maybeSingle() when zero rows is valid. Keep single() only when a missing row is a real bug.

faq.q: Why did this appear after I turned on RLS?
faq.a: RLS filters out rows the user may not see, so a query that used to return one row now returns zero.
